lxc_16c82b1fba1844f8.text: First, we look at greetings and how they show closeness.

lxc_4617eca9686b5042.text: Next, we look at French words that create polite distance, and at American small talk with strangers.

lxc_9b08b319bc9f6cb1.text: Then we explain why tipping matters so much in the USA.

lxc_a3b01072a4e04218.text: Last, we compare French and American meals.

lxc_3139d1ff5287b335.text: In Marseille, two old friends kiss on both cheeks.

lxc_c4f1ab85af322497.text: In Chicago, two people meet and choose a handshake or a hug.

lxc_d9b6fe455790a114.text: Earlier, we saw that the relationship chooses the greeting.

lxc_eff2480669781dc1.text: Here, we look at what happens when the greeting is missing, and at how body space works.

lxc_ef6f03c675031a47.text: A cheek kiss is an informal greeting.

lxc_bbe0c5a48b2cea01.text: It can show friendship, family ties, respect or comfort.

lxc_d6271311af24ecb5.text: So in places where cheek kissing is normal, the kiss carries a message.

lxc_38e548febc187525.text: If you do *not* kiss, people may read a message too.

lxc_7d46457f13188898.text: They can feel dislike or offense.

lxc_b352b61fd87055c2.text: France is not the same everywhere.

lxc_83e4378fe1b41c8d.text: The number of kisses changes from region to region.

lxc_27086fb16b2b2052.text: There is even a French joke: you can know which city you are in by counting the kisses.

lxc_344c69523fcc3301.text: In southern France, even two men often greet with cheek kisses.

lxc_c199db1e7bd6eaf8.text: In northern France, this happens less.

lxc_32d29857419d389a.text: So "the French kiss" is really many local habits.

lxc_15b1265c599e9d71.text: In some English-speaking countries, such as Australia and New Zealand, cheek kisses happen only among close friends, and handshakes or hugs are more common greetings.

lxc_41dd93db4c63f5b0.text: A handshake or a hug can do the same job as a kiss: it says how close two people are, but with a different kind of touch.

lxc_6665a1731b2e0cf9.text: Scientists who study space between people describe four zones: intimate, personal, social and public.

lxc_f2b85d56ef292df0.text: We let a person into a closer zone when we feel closer to them.

lxc_ca036df14cdf4eb7.text: Americans like about the same personal space as people in northern and central Europe.

lxc_6eb41e456f3fd523.text: In Japan, everyday greetings usually have less touching, so kisses, hugs and handshakes are less common than in many other places.

lxc_6406742807917e41.text: So a greeting is like a ruler.

lxc_b30152efa78ef7bd.text: It measures the relationship, and each culture marks the lines in a slightly different place.

lxc_91ef55340401a819.text: In France, you enter a bakery and say, "A baguette, please."

lxc_7ec755d100e09eae.text: The baker looks less friendly than before.

lxc_138f474489b68aaf.text: Saying *Bonjour* before any request is a basic rule of politeness in shops, cafés and bakeries.

lxc_9365c51dd038ad12.text: It helps you avoid a cold welcome.

lxc_1ed36493216cd4b5.text: People appreciate it even if it is the only French word you know.

lxc_71077a603e0a5593.text: The word comes first because it treats the worker as a person first and a service second.

lxc_5a18a374d6fed097.text: The French words *tu* and *vous* do a similar job.

lxc_c3b6529c5db9fbbc.text: Many languages have a choice like this.

lxc_22ee7b312fad3749.text: In the past, French speakers often used *tu* and *vous* in the same situations.

lxc_0db677fa4c0ddb27.text: It is less formal than *vous*, and it does not push people apart.

lxc_e24f322f084cc017.text: When a French person uses *vous* with you, it is not coldness.

lxc_dd4dd6fc98363659.text: Distance at the start is a polite way to say, "I take you seriously."

lxc_53ea3885b95b2282.text: In a line at an American supermarket, a stranger says, "Cold today, huh?"

lxc_d62ce42f0d405f01.text: You may never see this person again.

lxc_655f8b31ad239ffc.text: It shows strangers that you have friendly plans, not bad ones.

lxc_ac7287a27367b24c.text: It also keeps social bonds alive and helps people manage the distance between them.

lxc_99e06fb55798880c.text: Small talk works at the end of a talk too.

lxc_5835a04199da9a66.text: A few light words like "Have a good day!" make leaving softer, so it does not feel like rejection.

lxc_41c3986d1cf00507.text: So small talk is a tool for the edges of a relationship.

lxc_2b595072bf887cec.text: It lets two strangers be warm for one minute and then leave without any problem.

lxc_5d214174acbb6f14.text: This is why some visitors misunderstand Americans.

lxc_3863b21279e60942.text: They hear friendly words and expect a deep friendship.

lxc_119180bbec65bee4.text: But the friendly words are often a polite way to share a small, safe space.

lxc_c5e7c198cbc418c7.text: French politeness puts the respectful word, *Bonjour*, at the door.

lxc_7b55fbb708936bfc.text: American politeness often puts a light chat there.

lxc_38fcf8e33d38e415.text: Both are careful ways to handle a stranger.

lxc_2ca698aeaac2b42c.text: An American visitor in Paris leaves a big tip that nobody expected.

lxc_b5fdff8cc5b351cf.text: A French visitor in New York leaves no tip, and the server is upset.

lxc_90372614fa7041fe.text: Both made the same mistake from opposite sides.

lxc_d2e305d445a631f6.text: In 1919, Prohibition put money pressure on restaurants in the USA.

lxc_acb61e786d010ba5.text: So they accepted tips to add to their workers' pay.

lxc_d77b49f4a9f1221f.text: In this way, the tip slowly became part of the wage, not only a small extra "thank you."

lxc_fda3bb60af2379bf.text: That is why many American workers depend on tips.

lxc_22f7b60b2764d111.text: Tipping can feel awkward, because people are not sure how much to give.

lxc_9d0133318fd0e60d.text: It is also not always fair.

lxc_4e3c17d5a8954301.text: People sometimes tip by the price of the meal, not by the quality of the service.

lxc_22b30a1f65405462.text: And the system is hard to change.

lxc_8de48e71c675cfea.text: Some people argue that changing the tip rules could favor servers who get tips over staff who do not get tips, and make income less equal.

lxc_1959f6ca46e4da81.text: So in the USA, a tip is not a gift you can easily skip.

lxc_0eb1dee642d9df53.text: It is part of how workers get paid.

lxc_a3b9e5b193b7cf03.text: At lunchtime in Paris, office workers leave their desks to eat.

lxc_22298936840ac985.text: In many American towns, lunch may be a quick burger.

lxc_0b0f296412930bee.text: It is more useful to ask what each meal protects.

lxc_77bf2579fc1f5171.text: In France, enjoying food is an important value.

lxc_e4c1246234e6af50.text: In the 20th century, Georges Auguste Escoffier wrote down the rules of high French cooking.

lxc_62c55d6d5dbef434.text: Today, a lunch break usually lasts at least one hour.

lxc_fd33ed961bb899bb.text: Eating lunch at your desk is even illegal.

lxc_1b864b81f9dbc2eb.text: But a long lunch does not mean a big meal.

lxc_56d720b58b33725f.text: On busy workdays in Paris, lunches with many courses are not common.

lxc_260199b868cd426a.text: Many modern meals are simpler, and some dishes come from immigrant cooking.

lxc_d64137e197944c6f.text: Fast food and new habits among young people put pressure on the old food culture.

lxc_4f900bcb6edc8e60.text: Even so, France works to keep it, for example through education programs in schools.

lxc_28f7cca6b74efc13.text: American food grew from a different story.

lxc_c854b987df210ac6.text: US culture was shaped by history, geography and immigration.

lxc_a9515661cfcdcbb6.text: Famous foods like apple pie and hamburgers come from immigrant and local roots.

lxc_b53b68c0e273f19b.text: Fast food is a common part of American meals, and people worry that it adds calories and leads to health problems.

lxc_0240a8b7eab90500.text: So the French lunch protects time to enjoy food with others.

lxc_c84ac6128d47de4f.text: The quick American meal reflects a mixed food story and a busy day.
